BOPEN.heard: Building virtual environments exam prep, key terms, game AI decisions and systems. Thirty-three terms for the systems that make a game act on its own from state machines and behavior trees to seeded levels, learning from reward and networking. The exact term lets you tell an AI coding agent what to build.

BIDEA.heard: Hollow, this is Liam in for bear. Newcomers often think one distance is enough to make a guard start and stop chasing. It is not. With one threshold, a player at the edge makes the guard flicker. Two thresholds, one to start and a larger one to stop, give hysteresis. Game AI is full of pairs like that. This film goes through the terms group by group, each one shown.

BDEFS.heard: Six labels sit in the corners of the pictures that follow. In the book text, the course text uses and explains the term. In the glossary, the term is on the course term list, but the text does not explain it. Computed, the numbers are worked out on screen from stated inputs. Simulation, a model run step by step from stated rules, not a measurement of a real game. Illustrative data, numbers chosen to show the idea not measured. Conceptual, a drawing of the idea. With no data behind it.

B0101.heard: This table is the map, 33 terms about game AI, the code that makes characters decide in four groups. The first group is deciding with states, finite state machine, transition table, flicker and hysteresis. A character is in one mode at a time and something must stop it flipping.

B0102.heard: The second group is trees, scores, and plans. Behavior tree tick results, blackboard, condition, and action, selector, sequence, utility AI, weighted sum, goat, which is goal-oriented action planning and precondition and effect. These are three ways to decide what to do next.

B0103.heard: The third group is generating and checking. Seed, coherent noise, octave, determinism, height map, compute shader, validator, generate and test, constructive and safety margin. These terms cover making levels from a seed and proving they work.

B0104.heard: The fourth group is Learning and Networks, Reinforcement Learning, Reward, Discount Factor, Q-Learning, Epsilon-Greety, Authority, RPC, which is a remote procedure call and replication. These cover behavior learned from reward and states shared by two computers.

B0201.heard: A guard drawn as three boxes patrol, chase, and search with arrows between them. A finite state machine is a set of states with rules for leaving each one, and exactly one state is active at a time. In this scripted example, a row of distances carries the guard from patrol to chase to search and back to patrol. For example, the Walker guard is a finite state machine, and a label above it shows which state is current.

B0202.heard: The same four arrows now as rows. A transition table lists every state, the condition that moves it on and the state it moves to, one row per transition. The last column counts how often each row fired and search back to chase never fired. For example, the agent that built the Walker Guard was asked to write its transition table, from two in condition into the handoff file, so a reviewer can check every exit in one place.

B0203.heard: Now a seated noisy distance over 90 ticks with one threshold at 240. Flicker is rapid back and forth switching between states. Each time the noise crosses the line the guard switches and the red band blow marks chase. 37 switches so far. For example a player standing right at the edge of a guard's sight with only one radius would see the guard's label flip between chase and search over and over.

B0204.heard: Hysteresis means using two thresholds, one for switching on and another for switching off, so a small wobble cannot flip the state. Here the guard starts chasing under 220 and stops only over 260. On the same noisy signal, 37 switches become 3. For example, the Walker guard's lose radius is set larger than its sight radius, so a player hovering at the edge does not make it flicker.

B0301.heard: A tree with a selector at the top, two sequences, and a patrol action. A behavior tree is a tree of nodes that decides what a character does, and it is run again on every update. On this first tick, the player is visible, so they can see check succeeds, chase runs, and the selector stops there. For example, the Walker Guard's second brain is a behavior tree. Chase, if you can see the player, else search, else patrol.

B0302.heard: A tick is one update step in which the tree is evaluated again from the root. The facts change between ticks so the choice can change. Here tick one chooses chase, tick two search, and tick three patrol each time starting at the top. For example, the Walker-Gards tree gets one tick from its root on every physics frame, the same clock that moves the guard.

B0303.heard: Success, failure, and running are the three results a node can return. Running means not finished, tick me again. On tick two, the player is out of sight, so can see fails and its sequence fails. The second sequence finds a last position and search keeps running. Six of eight nodes were ticked and patrol never was. For example, a guard's walk to the last spot it saw the player returns running every tick until it arrives, then success.

B0304.heard: A blackboard is a shared memory of facts that the tree's nodes read and write. The box shows two facts on tick two. Player visible is false, which the can see check reads, and a last position, which the last position check reads. For example, the Walker-Gards tree keeps its blackboard in a dictionary, and the last known player position stored there is what sends the guard searching.

B0401.heard: Two rows of leaf results across six ticks. Condition and action are the two kinds of leaf. A condition asks a question and answers it once, success, or failure. An action does the work and may keep returning running. Here Chase returns running for three ticks and success on tick four when it arrives. For example, is the player in sight is a condition and walking to the spot where the player was last seen as an action.

B0402.heard: A selector also called a fallback tries its children in order and stops at the first one that does not fail. It is or with priority. In the top row the first child fails, the second succeeds and the third is skipped. If every child fails, the selector fails and if one is running, so is the selector. For example, a guards root selector says chase if you can, else search, else patrol.

B0403.heard: A sequence runs its children in order and stops at the first one that does not succeed. It is and with order, when all three succeed, the sequence succeeds. A failure in the middle stops it, and so does a child that is still running. A selector means or in a sequence means, and, for example, a guard's chase branch is a sequence. First can I see the player then chase, so it never chases what it cannot see.

B0501.heard: Three bars and three score curves in this made up example. Utility AI scores every option it is right now and picks the highest. As the player comes closer, the scores change and at 100 pixels with health 0.8, chase wins with 0.63. It makes one choice now not a plan. For example, an enemy that every moment scores attack, take cover and reload, then does whichever score's highest is Utility AI.

B0502.heard: A weighted sum adds several inputs, each multiplied by a weight that says how much it matters. Here each score adds a closeness part and a second weighted part. At 150 pixels in health 0.3, flee wins with 0.66. Raise health to 0.8 and chase wins with 0.51. For example, a boss could score calling for help as missing health times a big weight, plus nearby players times a small one.

B0601.heard: A goal and open door and four actions a search found to reach it. Go, goal-oriented action planning searches through possible actions for a sequence that makes the goal true. Under each action are the facts true after it. The search tried six world states. For example, a goblin told to get inside a locked hut could plan to fetch the key and open the door with no one scripting that order.

B0602.heard: Pre-condition and effect describe each action for the planner. The precondition is what must be true before the action can run, and the effect is what it changes. Open door needs has key in a door. After step two of the plan only at key and has key are true so open door is still blocked. For example, pulling a lever might need the character standing beside it as its precondition and have a lowered bridge as its effect.

B0701.heard: An agent in environment and a corridor of six cells. Reinforcement learning means learning behavior by trial and reward. The agent acts the environment answers with a new cell and a reward, and over many tries the agent learns what pays. Here on Step 5 it moves right into the goal and the episode ends. For example, the Walker Reinforcement Learning Lab trains an agent on a small grid to reach a goal and avoid two pits. With no path written by hand...

B0702.heard: A reward is the number the environment gives after each step, telling the agent how well it did. Here the first four steps each cost minus 0.01 and reaching the goal gives plus one. Add it up, they make the return plus 0.96. Reward is one step and return is the total. For example, in the Walker Grid lab, every ordinary step costs a little. A pit is punished and ends the episode and the goal pays the most.

B0703.heard: The discount factor written gamma sets how much a future reward is worth compared with one now. Each reward is multiplied by gamma once for every step it waits. With gamma 0.95 the gold reward still counts 0.815 and the discounted return is 0.78. With 0.5 only 0.063, for example. A low discount factor makes an agent grab a nearby coin instead of walking to a bigger

B0801.heard: A grid with two pits and a goal in this simulated run. Q Learning learns a value for each action in each state. A table of how good it is to go up, down, left, or right from every cell. The arrows show the best action after 500 episodes. From the red start, they reach the goal in eight steps and miss both pits. For example, the Walker Grid Lab prints an arrow grid like this from its Q table, written in plain GD script.

B0802.heard: Epsilon greedy is the rule for choosing moves while learning. With probability Epsilon take a random action, otherwise take the best one known. The black line is Epsilon falling from 1 to 0.05 so early moves are mostly random. The red line is success over the last 25 episodes, which first reaches 80% by the 313th episode. For example, an enemy learning to dodge sometimes tries a random direction. And that is how it finds a better one.

B0901.heard: Three strips of smooth noise in this simulated run, a seed is the number that fixes a random sequence. The values look random but are computed from the seed, which is why they are called pseudo-random. Seed 42 run twice gives the same strip with the largest difference of zero. Seed 7 gives a different one. For example, the Walker level generator takes a seed, so seed 7 builds the same level every time on the same engine version.

B0902.heard: Coherent noise is random, but it changes smoothly, so each value stays close to its neighbors. Pearlon and simplex noise are two kinds. The white noise on top jumps about. On average, neighbors differ by 0.61 in white noise and only 0.06 in coherent noise. For example, the Walker height map build starts from simplex noise, which gives its island smooth slopes instead of random speckles.

B0903.heard: An octave is one layer of noise at a set scale, added to other layers. Octave one is broad and strong. Octaves two and three are finer at half and a quarter of the strength. There some keeps the large shape and adds detail on top. For example, a mountain range and a height map gets its big peaks from the first octave and its rocky bumps from the finer ones.

B0904.heard: Determinism means the same inputs and the same seed give the same output on every run. Here each runs 64 numbers are boiled down to fingerprint. Seed 42 twice gives the same fingerprint. Seed 7 differs and so does Seed 42 once the generator itself changes. For example, the Walker height map build gives byte identical output for the same seed twice, but a level that must survive an engine upgrade should be saved as data.

B1001.heard: A pixeled island made from Seed 42. A height map is a grid with one height value at each position. Here noise is multiplied by a fade from the center outward, and every value under 0.2 becomes 0, which is C. 668 of the 1,536 cells are land. For example, the hills of an open world level can be stored as a gray image, where each pixel's brightness is the ground height at that spot.

B1002.heard: The Compute Shader is one program run on the GPU, the graphics processor over many cells at once separate from drawing. A loop fills 384 cells one after another, while the shader runs one copy of the formula per cell, none differ. You're both run on the CPU, the main processor, and in the course build the GPU result is still unchecked. For example, the Walker heightmap build writes its island formula twice. It has a GD script loop and has a compute shader.

B1101.heard: Two side views of a level checked by flood fill from the left. A validator is a check that tests generated content against rules. Here the rules are a climb of at most two and a jump of at most six columns. The top level is rejected at column 15 where the gap is too wide. The lower level is accepted, all 19 solid columns reached. For example, the Walker level validator reports the first column a player cannot reach and why.

B1102.heard: Generate 10 Test means making content at random, then checking each piece and throwing away whatever fails. 60 seeds, 1 square each and only 12 past 20%. With a policy of reject and reroll, 5 accepted levels took 20 seeds, so 15 were thrown away. For example, a dungeon generator that keeps rolling new room layouts until the validator finds a path from the entrance to the exit is Generate 10 Test.

B1103.heard: Constructive generation builds content by rules that make a bad result impossible. All 60 seeds pass so nothing is re-rolled. The validator still runs as the check that the rules worked. Generate and test rejects the bad and constructive generation never makes it. For example, a platformer generator that places each new platform within the player's jump range of the last one is constructive.

B1104.heard: A safety margin is extra room left, so generated content never only just passes. With the jump limit at 6 columns, 44 of 200 levels pass. With a margin of 1, the limit is 5 and 32 pass. The 12 in between need, the full jump, so a slightly short jump fails them. The margin of 1 is illustrative. For example, the Walker validators limits come from the player's measured jump, minus a margin the agent had to state.

B1201.heard: Two peers a host and a client each showing the same paddle. Authority is the part of the system allowed to change a value. Player one belongs to the host, Pier one. The client asks the host to move it to an absurd height, and the call is refused, so the host value stays 188.6. For example, in the Walker-Pong Lab, each paddle's owner reads its own keys, and only that owner may send the paddle's position.

B1202.heard: An RPC, a remote procedure call, is a function one computer asks another computer to run. Its mode says who may call it. The score function is open to any peer and all three client calls are accepted so the score goes from 0 to 3. The position function keeps the default mode, authority and all three calls are refused. For example, in a two player card game the client could ask the host by RPC to play a card and the host decides.

B1203.heard: Replication means copying a value from the peer that owns it to the other peers. The black line is the host's paddle height over 60 ticks, and the red steps are the client's copy. In this simulated run, values arrive three ticks late, and one packet in five is lost, so the copy lags by up to 13 pixels, then catches up. For example, the Walker Bomber build replicates each player's position to the other peers with a multiplayer synchronizer node.

B1301.heard: Each pair sets two look alike side by side. A selector tries children until one succeeds, so here it returns success and skips the rest. A sequence runs children until one fails, so here it returns failure. Selector is or and sequence is end.

B1302.heard: A finite state machine stores its exits on each state, so adding flee when hurt means a new state and three new exit edges. A behavior tree keeps priority in the order of the tree, so the same change is one new branch at the left.

B1303.heard: Generate and test makes levels at random and rejects the bad ones. For seeds 1 to 12, only 2 pass. Constructive generation builds each level so it cannot be bad and all 12 pass.

B1304.heard: Utility AI scores every option and picks the top one, a single choice made now. GOPE searches for plan toward a goal, here are four actions in order from going to the key to opening the door.

B1401.heard: A vague request sits above the exact instruction that replaces it. Stop the guard jittering becomes, start chasing under 220 pixels, and stop only over 260 two thresholds. On the same noisy signal, 37 switches become 3.

B1402.heard: Make the levels random but fair becomes, generate from a seed, run the validator, and reject any level that fails. In this run, 44 of 200 seeds pass and 156 are rejected.

B1403.heard: Make the AI choose sensibly becomes score every option from 0 to 1 using distance and health and take the highest. In this made up example at 150 pixels and health 0.8, Chase wins with 0.51.

B1404.heard: Make it repeatable becomes set seed 42 run twice and compare the output byte for byte. Both runs give the same fingerprint and seed 7 gives a different one. Same seed, same fingerprint.

B1405.heard: Don't let a client cheat becomes leave the RPC on Authority mode so the host checks who is calling. A score RPC opened to any peer accepted all three client calls. On Authority mode it accepted none.

B1501.heard: This is a checklist of six questions to ask before you trust a change to game AI. First, can the validator reject an impossible output, and what happens to that output then?

B1502.heard: Second, does the same seed give identical output twice on a pinned engine version. A seed reproduces a level only on the same generator.

B1503.heard: Third are the on and off thresholds different so the state cannot flicker. That is hysteresis, one distance to start chasing and a larger one to stop.

B1504.heard: Fourth, which node returned running on the last tick, and as its composite remember it, a composite with memory resumes that child and skips the checks to its left.

B1505.heard: Fifth, who has authority over this value and does the receiver check the caller. A function open to any peer trusts whoever calls it.

B1506.heard: 6. Does the test read only what can be observed, such as the guard's mode and position, never the machine's internals. Then say it exactly. Not make it fair, but validate every seed and reject failures.

BVDT.heard: Let's recap two thresholds on and off, give hysteresis and stop a state flickering. A selector is or with priority in a sequence is and with order. Utility AI scores every option now while GOPE searches for a plan. A reward is one step's number and the return adds them up over time. The same seed gives the same output and a validator rejects levels that fail. Authority says who may change a value and replication copies it to others.

BHTF.heard: Quizmy on game AI terms with short game-making cases one at a time. Use Hysteresis Flicker Selector, Sequence Utility AI, Goat, Reward, Generate and Test, Constructive Generation and Authority. For each case I must name the exact term and say why its look alike is wrong. Hold back the answer until I reply then tell me if I was right.

BOUT.heard: Key terms, game AI decisions and systems at Nick Bear Brown.
